sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraphs on the 7 January 1914 completion of a staged crossing by the old French crane boat Alexandre La Valley and the inauguration with John A. Constantine serving as pilot aboard Ancon.

Report of Electrical and Mechanical Engineer, pp. 115–116, “Up lockage of tug Gatun” and its return. Measured lift 64.7 feet. Pp. 118–119, first passage of the west chamber at Pedro Miguel by La Valley with Clapet No. 9 and barge No. 6, and trial at Gatún by the Ancon on 11 June.

Paragraphs on lock steps and origin of construction cement, gravity and locomotives. Concluding paragraphs cover shovels 222 and 230 on 20 May 1913, locomotive 260 on 10 September, the Gatun tug on 26 September and Marmot’s December cut at Cucaracha.

Description of the canal, pp. 46–48, Gatun Lake, Gaillard Cut, Miraflores Lake and Locks. The bottom was 40 ft above sea level and the lake provided a channel 45 ft deep. P. 48 describes the paired chambers, three flights and the effect of Pacific tides on the lift at Miraflores.

The New Encyclopedic Atlas and Gazetteer of the World (1914), p. 66. Map of the route through Gatún Lake and the cut to the Pacific locks, with the railway, grid index, settlement names and coastal approaches.

Governor’s report, discussion of Gaillard Cut slides and general reopening on 15 April 1916. Appendix E, plates 45, 48, 50, 54 and 56, shows the September working face and subsequent obstruction. “Lockages”, p. 76, records about forty southbound vessels returning through Gatún.

Paragraphs on rail transport of spoil to Gatún Dam and the Naos–Flamenco breakwater, on extending the lake across the divide, and on the distinct modes of slope movement in the Culebra and Cucaracha slides.
